This is the main text for the Feast of the Transfiguration in many liturgical traditions, as it sets the stage for the divine revelation that occurs six days later.

Matt 16:24-28 concerns the Son of Man coming in his Father's glory to 'reward each person according to what they have done' (v. 27). This is a direct reference to the final judgment and Christ's return. Verses 24-26 establish the premises for judgment by defining discipleship as a path through suffering, which is central to the message of Last Sunday.

Matt 16:24-26 with the call to 'take up one's cross' and 'deny oneself' is a key text for Lent and repentance. It defines discipleship as a path through suffering and self-denial. Although this is often read on Transfiguration Sunday, the primary liturgical context here is the introduction to Christ's Transfiguration, so its relevance is secondary in this specific tagging.

The text in Matt 16:1-4 about 'the sign of Jonah' is a direct foreshadowing of Jesus' suffering and resurrection (Jonah in the belly of the fish as an image of three days in the tomb). This is a central theme on Palm Sunday, which marks the beginning of Holy Week and the way to the cross.

Matt 16:21-23 contains Jesus' first prediction of his suffering ('must go to Jerusalem and suffer... be killed'). This is the theological key to Palm Sunday, which celebrates Jesus' entry into Jerusalem with full awareness that this leads to crucifixion. Peter's reaction ('God forbid') highlights the conflict between human expectations of a conquering hero and God's plan of suffering.

In many liturgical traditions (especially in the Catholic and some Lutheran churches), Matt 16:21-23 (or its parallel in Mark 8) is the main text for Transfiguration Sunday. The text marks the decisive turning point in the Gospels where Jesus clearly preaches his suffering, and Peter attempts to prevent it. This sets the course toward Lent and the cross.

Matt 16:24-26 with the call to 'take up one's cross' and 'deny oneself' is a key text for Lent and repentance. It defines discipleship as a path through suffering and self-denial, which is at the heart of the message on Transfiguration Sunday and during Lent.

Matt 16:27-28 concerns the Son of Man coming in his Father's glory to 'reward each person according to what they have done'. This is a direct reference to the final judgment and Christ's return, which is the main theme of Last Sunday (Christ the King).

Verse 28 ('Some standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom') is often interpreted as a direct foreshadowing of Christ's Transfiguration, which occurs six days later (Matt 17). The Transfiguration is a preview of the glory mentioned here.
